<reason>B establishes a plausible, person-directed emergency exception and explains why it defeats the universal prohibition without licensing routine deprivation. B directly answers the reliability, notice, and scope questions. A's historical examples establish serious risks, but its assertion that those systems contained all B's safeguards is unsupported. A also blurs its own rule by permitting guaranteed later review while denying that the initial withholding rests solely on the flag. B more convincingly distinguishes automatic restoration from indefinite suspension pending investigation.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B decisively answers A's closing capacity dilemma: reviewing every flagged case before imminent disbursement requires different capacity from prevalidated models, automated notice and expiry, and prioritized hardship assistance. B also exposes A's asymmetric assumption that mandatory prior review is enforceable but mandatory restoration must fail.</best_rebuttal>
